newsitem.title: UK: Funds say budget means rate threat for UK markets.
newsitem.headline: Funds say budget means rate threat for UK markets.

text.p: A cut in corporate taxes in Wednesday's UK budget will partly offset the abolition of corporation tax credits but the threat of rising interest rates will hang over both gilt and equity markets, British-based fund managers said.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown announced a cut in the corporate tax rate of two percent to 31 percent but also abolished the Advanced Corporation Tax (ACT) credit enjoyed by pension funds.
Institutional investors voiced concern that the budget did not do enough to dampen the inflationary pressures from rampant consumer spending.

"I think it was on balance equity unfriendly, particularly if the bond market is not going to believe the public sector borrowing requirement forecast," said Nick Knight, strategist at Nomura Securities.

"The other negative is that they didn't do enough to prove their financial rigour by attacking the consumer," said Knight."Short rates will have to go up which means sterling goes up - another negative for equities."
The abolition of ACT, which gave benefits to tax-exempt investors which held equities, will tend to push pension fund investors towards the gilt market, fund managers said.
"ACT is the worst of the markets' fears, but that has been in the market for some time," said Mike Grimble, chief strategist at Norwich Union Investment Management.
"In the medium term it will be good for gilts, but a lot of that rotation has already happened," said Johnathan Cunliffe, fixed-income specialist at fund manager Lombard Odier.
Grimble said he is not convinced that the abolition of ACT credit and the cut in corporate tax will lead to further investment.
"There may be some pressure from investors to raise dividends," he said.
Institutional investors say they will have to sharpen their pencils to work out which economic sectors will be hit and which may benefit.
Of most concern, fund managers say, is the damage that strong sterling could do to British exporters if interest rates rise again.
"There has been a distinct absence of measures to dampen final demand in the UK economy against a backdrop of very buoyant consumer spending," said Cunliffe.
Michael Hughes, global strategist at BZW, said he thinks the budget painted a credible picture for investors but agrees that gilts may be damaged by the prospect of rate rises.

"I would guess it is probably going to be taken better for equities than gilts, partly because there is still a risk of interest rates rising. The offset of the corporate tax cut is relief for equities despite the ACT credit cut but that is not there for gilts."

"(Brown) hasn't hit the consumer spending side as much as had been anticipated. You are going to have to look at an interest rate rise to go with this and to that extent the gilt market is going to feel somewhat constrained."
Knight of Nomura is fairly negative on equities, seeing a selloff of about 100 points over the next several days.
"I'd prefer the price we were at Monday night rather than Wednesday night," he said.
